title: Progressive Disclosure of MCP Tools and Tool Descriptions

concepts.heading: Why raw tool dumps cost context
concepts.body: Databricks documents the Model Context Protocol as the way an agent queries data, searches documents and calls external services. Databricks-provided MCP servers (Genie One, GitHub, Slack and others), registered servers and custom servers hosted on Databricks Apps all expose tools, and each tool arrives with a name, a description and an input schema. If the agent loads every definition from every server at the start, those schemas travel in every model call whether or not the request uses them. That spends the attention budget before the user's question is read and leaves less room for the task. A tool result is context too: a generic SQL tool that returns four thousand rows pushes them all into the window and leaves the arithmetic to the model. A purpose-built tool that aggregates in the warehouse and returns three rows is cheaper and more reliable. The wording progressive disclosure, scoping tool results and attention budget is the exam guide's vocabulary and generally accepted context-engineering practice. The Databricks docs do not define it as a setting.

concepts.heading: The staged approach and its cost
concepts.body: Progressive disclosure loads tool information in stages, each adding only what the next decision needs. Stage one is a compact index: a name plus a one-line purpose for each tool or server. Stage two happens after the agent selects a tool: a lookup step returns that tool's full parameter schema. Stage three is the call itself, whose result should also be scoped, for example a list of order ids and statuses plus a separate detail call for one order. Count it: a catalog of 60 tools at about 500 tokens per schema costs 30,000 tokens as a dump. Staged, it costs 60 index lines of about 20 tokens plus 3 schemas, about 2,700 tokens. The price is one extra round trip per tool used. The agent also has to know the protocol, so a few lines in the prompt must say that the index is not enough to call a tool and that the lookup comes first. Without it the agent guesses arguments and gets validation errors.

concepts.heading: Hot tools and permitted tools
concepts.body: Staging is a trade of steps for tokens, so it should not cover everything. Tools used in nearly every conversation, such as order lookup in a support chat, belong in the always-loaded layer: deferring them adds a round trip every time and saves little. Rarely used tools in the long tail go behind the index. A second lever is simply not exposing tools nobody may call. The Databricks MCP page states that Databricks-provided and registered MCP servers use Unity Catalog permissions, and that governing an MCP includes sharing access and restricting tools. If callers may use 18 of 30 tools, restrict the agent to those 18: the other 12 definitions leave every call, the model cannot select them, and no tokens go to permission errors. Widening access to stop the errors breaks least privilege, and a prompt line listing forbidden tools leaves the definitions in the window. Choosing the smallest useful tool set as a context strategy is the exam's convention, not a documented Databricks feature.

concepts.heading: Ambiguous tool descriptions
concepts.body: The model picks a tool mainly from its name and description, and fills arguments from parameter names and descriptions. When two descriptions say nearly the same thing, nothing separates them and the choice becomes close to random. Overlap takes several forms. Two near-identical sentences, such as one tool looking up customer information and another retrieving account information for a customer. A superset tool, such as a billing history tool whose description is the union of an invoice tool and a payments tool. Identical names from different servers, such as a generic search tool on both GitHub and Slack. Parameters both described as the id. Read the descriptions as the model does and ask which ones fit a sample question. The fix is to state what the tool returns, its key input, when to prefer it and when not to, plus formats such as a C- or ACC- prefix. Random names, identical text or a rule to choose freely do not separate anything. Overlap analysis is exam vocabulary, not a Databricks-defined term.

examPoints: Progressive disclosure shows a compact tool index first and loads a tool's full schema only after the agent selects it, so tool tokens follow the tools used, not the tools that exist; the cost is an extra round trip, and the agent must be told the protocol.

Keep frequently used tools always loaded, put the long tail behind the index, restrict the tools exposed to those the callers may use under Unity Catalog permissions, and scope tool results (aggregate server-side, return a summary plus a detail call).

Confusing tools are fixed by contrastive descriptions: what each returns, its input and format, when to use it instead of the neighbor, and system or item type for same-named tools; renaming to meaningless names or duplicating text does not help.

quiz.q: An agent reaches 60 registered tools and every model call starts with all their names, descriptions and schemas. The team adopts progressive disclosure. What does the window hold before the agent has picked a tool?
choices: The full schemas of the ten most used tools, with the other fifty hidden until requested by exact name
A compact index of tool names and one-line descriptions, with a full schema fetched only after selection
Only the user's question, so the agent has to guess a tool name and learn its parameters from the error
Every full schema with the parameter descriptions removed, so that all 60 tools fit in a smaller footprint
quiz.explain: The first stage is a short index that answers which tool to use; the full schema is loaded for the chosen tool only. Hiding all tool information leaves nothing to choose from, and stripped schemas still load every tool.

quiz.q: An agent has find_customer ("Looks up customer information.") and get_account ("Retrieves account information for a customer."). It calls them almost at random for a billing address question. Which change fixes the confusion?
choices: Add the same worked example call for both tools to the system prompt so the model sees how each one is invoked
Rename the tools tool_a and tool_b so that the names cannot suggest anything that might mislead the model
Append synonyms of customer and account to both descriptions so that every question matches both strongly
Rewrite each description to state what it returns, its key input and when to use it instead of the other tool
quiz.explain: The descriptions overlap, so the fix is contrastive wording that tells the model which tool returns the billing address and which input each needs. The same example, meaningless names or more synonyms leave nothing that separates the tools.

recap: Tool definitions and tool results are context: stage them with a compact index, a schema lookup and scoped results, keep hot tools loaded, expose only permitted tools, and write contrastive descriptions. Progressive disclosure is the exam's term, not a Databricks setting.

title: Clearing Tool Results, Unity Catalog Function Tools and Agent Skills

concepts.heading: Which raw tool results can be cleared
concepts.body: In a long task the largest items in the message history are usually raw tool outputs, and they matter most in the turn that produced them. Clearing a tool result means removing its bulky payload from the window. The terms tool result clearing and message history pressure belong to the exam guide and to generally accepted context-engineering practice. The Databricks docs do not define them. A result is a good candidate when it is large and nothing the task still needs exists only inside it. Candidates are a 30,000-character JSON whose three order ids and totals are already written into the plan, a broad query superseded by a narrower one, and a 9,000-token column listing after the agent chose two tables and noted their columns. Poor candidates are a small result holding the only copy of a value the final answer must report, the user's region used as a filter in every remaining step, and the result of the call made one step ago that the agent has not analyzed yet. Size alone does not decide; dependence does.

concepts.heading: Clearing policies that keep a way back
concepts.body: Clearing is a policy as well as a technique. Decide how soon each result is needed again. An inventory agent that diffs each new result against the previous two keeps the three newest in full and replaces the older ones with placeholders. Clearing the newest results, keeping all forty, or clearing everything immediately each fail in a different way. The placeholder matters: if a cleared result leaves no trace, the history looks as if the call never happened and the agent repeats it. A placeholder names the tool, the arguments and the key findings, which costs a few tokens. When the raw rows are also stored in a Delta table, the placeholder can hold the table name, the row count and the findings, and the agent can reload exact rows later with a just-in-time query. Truncating a JSON to its first characters, summarizing and discarding the table, or moving rows into the system prompt do not keep that path back. Prompt rules such as never call a tool twice break legitimate refreshes. These policies are generally accepted practice, not Databricks features.

concepts.heading: Choosing a Unity Catalog function as a tool
concepts.body: The Databricks page on agent tools with Unity Catalog functions says to use them when the agent needs to run predefined logic, such as a SQL query whose parameters the agent supplies, and to start with MCP servers for other tools. Calling an existing function needs EXECUTE on it plus USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA on its parent catalog and schema, so access is governed in Unity Catalog. Registered functions have named parameters and a return type, so a choice can be judged from them. Ask three things. Functional fit: does the tool do the step, such as a calc_discount function when the agent already holds the order total and tier. Input and output compatibility: can the agent supply every parameter from what it has, and does the output match the next tool's parameter, such as an ISO 8601 string for a start_time STRING. Task requirements: a fixed approved calculation with region and quarter parameters beats a tool that accepts any SQL text. Prefer narrow typed inputs, allowed values and small returns, such as a single status value, over free-text filters or whole-table returns. Narrow-input design is generally accepted practice.

concepts.heading: Packaging rarely used instructions as Agent Skills
concepts.body: The Databricks page on extending Genie Code with agent skills says skills follow the open Agent Skills standard and package domain-specific knowledge and workflows, with guidance, best practices, reusable code and executable scripts. Unlike custom instructions, which are applied globally, skills are loaded automatically and only in the relevant context, based on the request and the skill's description. That keeps the context window efficient, which is why a rarely used procedure belongs in a skill and not in an always-on prompt. Each skill has its own folder with a required SKILL.md whose frontmatter has a name and a description, then Markdown instructions; scripts and reference files go in the folder and are referenced by relative paths. The docs give a workspace skill example of PII handling that masks sensitive columns. The description is the loading trigger, so vague wording causes both missed and false loads, and the docs advise clear names and descriptions and focused skills. Rules that apply to every request, such as tone or confidentiality, stay in the always-on instructions. Calling this progressive disclosure is the exam's framing.

examPoints: Clear a raw tool result only when it is large and what the task needs is already captured elsewhere; superseded and already extracted results qualify, while a sole copy of a needed value or the latest unanalyzed result does not.

Replace cleared results with placeholders naming the tool, arguments and key findings, keep the newest results the next step compares in full, and for results stored in Delta put the table name in the placeholder so the agent can query again.

Choose a Unity Catalog function tool by functional fit and input/output compatibility with narrow typed parameters; package rarely used workflows as skills (SKILL.md with name and description, loaded when relevant) and keep rules for every request in the system prompt.

quiz.q: A research agent nears its context limit. The history holds a 30,000-character JSON from get_orders returned 25 turns ago. The three order ids and totals needed from it are already in the agent's plan, and the raw JSON will not be used again. Which action frees space without hurting the task?
choices: Clear the raw result, keep the plan entries and leave a short note of the call
Truncate the JSON to its first 2,000 characters so part of every old result stays available
Clear the agent's reasoning messages from the last ten turns, since reasoning matters less than data
Delete the plan entries together with the JSON, because the plan only repeats what the JSON contained
quiz.explain: The needed facts live in the plan, so the bulky payload can go while a short note records the call. Truncation leaves partial data, reasoning may hold unrecorded decisions, and deleting the plan removes the only copy of the facts.

quiz.q: A team packaged a data-quality workflow as a skill whose description reads "Helpful workflow stuff." The agent ignores it for data-quality requests and sometimes applies it to unrelated tasks, although the SKILL.md instructions are correct. What fixes the loading behavior?
choices: Merge it with the team's other skills into one large skill, so that the agent only has a single description to match
Copy the instructions into the system prompt as well, so that they apply whatever the description says
Rewrite the name and description to say what the skill does and when to use it, for one workflow
Move every referenced script into SKILL.md so that the skill loads as one file
quiz.explain: The agent decides from the name and description whether to load a skill, so a specific description fixes both misses and false loads. Merging, duplicating into the prompt or inlining scripts all increase context or blur the trigger.

recap: Clear large raw tool results once their needed facts are captured, and leave placeholders with a path back. Pick Unity Catalog function tools by fit and compatibility, and move rarely used workflows into skills with precise descriptions.

title: Compaction: Finding Lost Information and Tuning the Prompt

concepts.heading: What compaction is, and what it loses
concepts.body: Compaction replaces older history with a summary so a long task can continue inside the window. The exam guide's terms, compaction, summarization and trimming, are generally accepted context-engineering practice; the Databricks docs do not define compaction or describe a compaction prompt, so treat them as the exam's vocabulary and not as a Databricks feature. A summarizer left without guidance tends to keep the narrative and drop exact strings, because they look like detail. The symptoms after compaction point to what was dropped. An agent that asks again for a stack trace and file path lost exact strings. An agent that writes to orders_prod after being told to work only in orders_dev lost a constraint. An agent that stops and asks what to do next lost its remaining steps. An agent that repeats a failed approach lost negative results. An agent that cannot give a growth rate lost exact figures. Every one is a category of information that a paraphrase cannot rebuild.

concepts.heading: Diagnose, then revise the prompt
concepts.body: The efficient order of work has three steps. First compare the summary with the raw history, which an MLflow trace preserves, and name the category that is missing. Second, change the compaction prompt so that this category is required: keep error messages, paths and identifiers verbatim; keep the user's goal, constraints and prohibitions stated explicitly; include a section for current state and remaining steps in order; list approaches tried and why they failed; keep figures with units and labels. Third, re-run and check that the failing questions are now answerable. Each fix adds a few lines to the summary, so the token cost barely moves. Wrong turns are easy to name. Making the summary shorter or friendlier does not restore data. Compacting earlier removes more detail. Deleting the oldest turns has no judgment. Rounding numbers destroys the values. A generic warning in the system prompt does not name the table that was lost. Telling the agent to refuse the question hides the symptom.

concepts.heading: Tuning order: recall first, then precision
concepts.body: Define two measures on a saved trace. Recall is the share of facts that later steps need which survive in the summary, for example 34 of 40 is 85 percent. Precision is how much of the summary is useful, with repeated or superfluous output counting against it, for example 8 of 20 sentences only restate earlier ones. The exam guide's order is to maximize recall first and then improve precision. A short summary hides what is missing, while noise in a long summary is easy to see and cut, so trimming before recall is complete only hides the gaps. In practice, build a checklist of the facts each trace's later steps use and score every revision against it. Change one instruction at a time on the same traces so an effect can be tied to a change. Include varied traces, not only one clean run. When a precision edit such as drop redundant tool output costs an order id, narrow the rule to duplicates and failed output and add a keep list for identifiers. Do not revert everything. This method is generally accepted practice, not a documented Databricks procedure.

concepts.heading: Trimming heuristics or real compaction
concepts.body: A hard-coded trimming rule, such as keep the last 15 messages or drop tool results older than 10 steps, needs no extra model call and behaves the same way every time. It is enough when relevance follows a simple pattern, usually recency. A FAQ agent answering independent questions fits, and so does a nightly batch where only the status line at a known position of each log matters; a parser can keep that line and clear the rest. It fails when relevance depends on content, not age. A migration agent that learned in step 2 that dates are stored in local time needs that fact in step 70, and a user correction from the first third of a run must survive whenever it was given. Window pressure alone does not justify a new approach, since every long run fills the window. The deciding fact is the information relevance pattern. Mixed histories can use a hybrid: a rule clears used tool outputs, and a content-aware compaction keeps the small dialogue of constraints. Raising the window size or changing N only delays the loss.

examPoints: After a compaction failure, compare the summary with the raw history, name the dropped category (exact strings, constraints, remaining steps, failed approaches, figures) and require that category in the compaction prompt without making the summary much longer.

Tune recall first (capture everything later steps need, scored against a checklist of facts from saved traces), then improve precision (merge repeated output, drop retries), one change at a time on the same traces, and narrow a precision rule that costs recall instead of reverting it.

Use a trimming heuristic when relevance follows recency or a fixed structure; use content-aware compaction when an early finding or correction can matter late, and combine the two when the history has parts with different patterns.

quiz.q: A migration agent was told in turn 3: "Do not touch orders_prod; work only in orders_dev." After its history was compacted the agent wrote to orders_prod. The summary said only "the user asked for a migration of the orders tables." What should change in the compaction step?
choices: Add "be careful with production tables" to the system prompt and leave the compaction prompt as it is
Remove every user message from the summarizer's input, since user messages are the source of conflicting instructions
Raise the sampling temperature so the agent tries different actions after each compaction step
Require the summary to keep the user's goal, constraints and prohibitions, stated explicitly with table names
quiz.explain: The constraint was lost in compaction, so the compaction prompt must name constraints as a category to keep. A generic warning does not name the table, and dropping user messages or adding randomness removes or ignores the rule.

quiz.q: After two tuning rounds a compaction prompt keeps every fact that later steps use in five sample traces, but summaries repeat the same verbose query output three times and include full retry text. What is the right next iteration?
choices: Remove the instruction listing what to preserve so that the summarizer can drop the noisy output itself
Add instructions that merge repeated output and drop retry text, then re-check the same traces
Replace the prompt with a rule that keeps only the last ten messages of the history in every case
Raise the maximum summary size so the repeated text fits, since the facts are already preserved
quiz.explain: Recall is acceptable, so the next step is a targeted precision edit followed by a re-check that no needed fact vanished. Removing the keep list or switching to a last-N rule risks recall, and a larger cap accepts the noise.

recap: Compaction failures show up as a missing category of information, so diagnose against the raw trace and require that category in the prompt. Tune recall before precision with measurable checks, and use fixed trimming only when relevance follows a regular pattern.

title: What to Keep, What to Drop and Aggressive vs Conservative Compaction

concepts.heading: Load-bearing content versus safe-to-remove content
concepts.body: Content is safe to remove during compaction when no downstream step depends on it, because it is repeated, because its useful part was extracted and the way to reproduce it is kept, or because it is metadata nobody reads. Content is load-bearing when a later step reads it. The categories below are the exam guide's convention and generally accepted practice; the Databricks docs do not define a keep list. Keep: user instructions, corrections and prohibitions that are still active; identifiers and values a later call will use, such as a transaction id returned 12 turns ago; open plan steps; decisions with their reasons; records of failed approaches. Usually removable: raw HTML or a 3,000-row result already reduced to the needed figures with the query text kept; identical boilerplate prepended to every tool result after the first copy; pleasantries. An age rule that deletes old tool output can destroy the only copy of a pending value, so extract such values into the summary before clearing the output.

concepts.heading: Operational metadata and how to prove removal is safe
concepts.body: Some content exists for the developer, not the agent. A wrapper that appends latency_ms, tokens and request_id to every tool result adds tokens that no later step reads. The Databricks tracing overview states that MLflow Tracing records the inputs, outputs, latency, token usage and cost of every intermediate step, so the same data survives outside the context window and removing it from the agent's history costs nothing. The test is simple: does any downstream step read it, and does a better record exist? To prove it for a new category, such as retrieved passages the agent quotes in earlier answers, do not rely on size, age or the model's own opinion. Size says nothing about dependence, old passages can be cited again, and a model's self-report about its needs is unreliable. Replay saved traces with the category removed and compare downstream steps and final answers with the originals; a changed step or answer means the removal is unsafe. MLflow evaluation on a fixed set of traces makes that comparison repeatable. This replay method is generally accepted practice.

concepts.heading: Aggressive versus conservative compaction
concepts.body: Compaction posture is a trade between tokens and fidelity. Aggressive compaction compresses hard: fewer tokens on every later call, lower cost and latency, but a higher chance of losing a subtle qualifier, an exception or a negation. Conservative compaction keeps more detail: higher fidelity, but longer summaries that cost more on each call and use more of the attention budget. Neither guarantees correct answers, and neither removes the need to measure downstream accuracy. The right posture follows the cost of an error against the cost of tokens. A triage agent classifying thousands of low-stakes tickets per hour, where a missed detail costs a minor re-ask, should compress aggressively. A claims agent where a missed exclusion clause can cause a wrong payout should keep clauses and qualifiers verbatim and accept the cost. Neither extreme is mandatory. The posture is the exam's convention, and the Databricks docs set no compaction level.

concepts.heading: Tiered compaction and deciding with data
concepts.body: Between the extremes, a tiered prompt compresses by category. Pin what is costly to lose, such as clauses, exceptions, constraints and identifiers, verbatim, and compress routine narrative and bulk output hard. Since most tokens in a trace are routine, most of the savings remain while the dangerous losses are blocked. Alternating postures on a timer, compressing the first half hard, running conservative compaction on every call while halving the documents read, or having a human review summaries all fail: losses depend on content, older material is where an early clause sits, and reviewers cannot restore details that are no longer in the summary. To choose a level for a new agent, use data. Run the same saved tasks at several compaction levels with MLflow evaluation, whose traces record token usage and cost for each step, compare task success with token cost, and choose the cheapest level that meets the quality bar. Copying another agent's posture or picking the best-written summaries does not measure that. The decision rule is the exam's convention.

examPoints: Keep active constraints and corrections, pending identifiers and values, open plan steps, decisions and failed approaches; remove duplicates, boilerplate, pleasantries and raw output whose conclusion and reproduction path are kept; extract values before clearing by age.

Operational metadata that no step reads, such as latency and token lines, is safe to remove because MLflow Tracing records latency, token usage and cost; prove a new category is safe by replaying saved traces without it and comparing downstream steps and answers.

Aggressive compaction fits low-stakes, high-volume work; conservative fits costly errors; a tiered prompt pins critical categories verbatim and compresses the rest, and the level is chosen by comparing task success and token cost on the same tasks.

quiz.q: An agent's wrapper appends a debug line such as latency_ms=412 tokens=1860 request_id=7f3a to every tool result. The lines are a sizeable share of the history, no later step reads them, and MLflow Tracing records the same information. Can they be removed during compaction?
choices: No, because request ids must stay in the history for the agent to resend a request when a call fails
Yes, because no step reads them and MLflow Tracing already records latency, token usage and cost
Yes, but only after the agent has repeated each figure in its own words so that a copy of every value remains
No, because latency and token figures can change the agent's choice of tool and must stay in the history
quiz.explain: The lines are unread by the agent and a better record exists in the trace, so removing them saves tokens at no cost. Restating them keeps the noise, and retries and tool choice do not depend on these figures here.

quiz.q: A long-running legal-research agent reads dozens of documents. Aggressive compaction was cheap but sometimes lost an exception clause. Conservative compaction fixed that but doubled token cost. Which design keeps most of the savings and the safety?
choices: Run conservative compaction on every call, and halve the number of documents the agent reads in each session
Compress aggressively in the second half of each task and conservatively in the first half
Compact aggressively, but keep clauses, exceptions and constraints verbatim and compress routine text
Alternate aggressive and conservative compaction on a timer, so the average cost falls between the two
quiz.explain: Pinning the costly categories verbatim blocks the observed failure while routine content still shrinks. The other designs cut coverage, compress old clauses or merely average the risk without regard to content.

recap: Remove what no later step reads or what is captured and reproducible, keep constraints, pending values, open steps and failed approaches, and verify by replaying traces. Choose aggressive or conservative compaction by the cost of an error, usually tiered, and decide with task success against token cost.
